rashi:a1.1: If one rendered another’s pure items impure and died, they did not penalize his son after him: to pay, even though they did penalize him himself, as we say in the chapter Arba’a Avot Nezikin (Bava Kamma 4b).
rashi:a1.2: That is not evident: for the pure items lie before him, and no damage is evident in them.
rashi:a1.3: Is not considered damage: so as to make him liable by Torah law, even himself.
rashi:a2.1: Mishna. And its hair dangling: because it had never been shorn.
rashi:a2.3: What is the status of this: that they let it grow so old.
rashi:a2.5: And they permitted it: for one cannot say that this gentile intended to make it permitted, since he does not know that it would be slaughtered on account of a blemish that he makes in it, [he knows only that it is slaughtered] if one befalls it by itself.
rashi:a3.1: Any that is intentional: where he intended to inflict a blemish in order to make it permitted.
rashi:a4.1: Gemara. For had it taught us only the gentile: that they permitted the first firstborn [blemished] through him, because one cannot say this gentile will come to acquire the habit of inflicting blemishes on consecrated animals. A gentile’s habit does not concern us, for he is accustomed to what is prohibited anyway.
rashi:a5.1: And will not come to confuse with an adult: one who sees that the Sages permitted on account of a blemish that came through children will not come to say that if an adult inflicts a blemish it is permitted, for an adult is not confused with a minor.
rashi:a6.1: They taught only: that the firstborn is permitted through the gentile.
rashi:a6.2: Only where they said to him: to the quaestor, “It is not slaughtered unless it had a blemish,” which implies that a blemish will befall it by itself. So one cannot say that the gentile learned from their words that they would like him to inflict a blemish on it.
rashi:a6.3: Was caused: implies through a person.
rashi:a7.1: It is by itself: for the gentile did not know that it would become permitted through him, and he did not intend to make it permitted.
rashi:a8.1: An indirect action: if he placed dough or a pressed fig on the firstborn’s ear so that a dog would come and take it.
rashi:a9.1: Speaks offhandedly: the quaestor did not ask them what its status was; rather they themselves spoke offhandedly and said, “See, this one will never be slaughtered except through a blemish,” and they did not intend that he inflict a blemish on it.
rashi:a10.1: Mishna. If a firstborn was [pursuing him]: a goring ram pursuing a person to gore him, and the person kicked the firstborn and made a blemish in it.
rashi:a10.2: He may slaughter on its account: even a priest, since he intended to save himself.
rashi:a12.1: Gemara. His distress: that it pursued him.
rashi:a14.1: Before it emerges into the air of the world: for a firstborn is not sacred until the womb sanctifies it.
rashi:a14.2: A kid, on its ear: a kid’s ears are long, and before its whole head emerges its ears are visible, and he can inflict a blemish; for as long as its whole head has not emerged it is not considered born.
rashi:a14.3: A lamb, on its lip: for its lips are visible first, while its ears are bound [against its head] and are not visible until its whole head has emerged.
rashi:a14.4: Its temples: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a15.1: It eats and it is not visible: if the firstborn has a blemish inside its mouth, and when it eats it is not visible, nevertheless, since when it cries out it is visible, it is an exposed blemish and it is slaughtered on its account. For we say in the coming chapter (Bekhorot 37a) that it is slaughtered only for an exposed blemish.
rashi:a15.2: Pa’ei: it cries out and opens its mouth wide.
rashi:a15.3: The external ḥutin: the gums of the teeth, (Rashi adds an Old French gloss). The external ones are those in front, opposite its nose, which were damaged, with a little missing from them.
rashi:a15.4: Or that were scratched: cut across their width from above, in depth, without anything missing. It is a blemish, since those gums are visible.
rashi:a15.5: The internal ones: in which the large teeth are set, (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a15.6: That were extracted: entirely, it is a blemish, as he goes on to explain, since when it cries out it is visible. But damage or scratching is not noticeable in them, for they are hidden in the mouth.
rashi:a16.1: What is the reason: that the internal ones are a blemish, even [only] when uprooted.
rashi:a17.1: Mishna. That are capable of being brought about by a person: where one can say a person inflicted it, for example its eye was blinded, its foreleg was cut off, its ear was slit.
rashi:a17.2: Israelite shepherds are deemed credible: to say that they befell it by themselves.
rashi:a17.3: Priest-shepherds are not deemed credible: for they are suspect in the matter. The Gemara explains what it calls Israelite shepherds and what it calls priest-shepherds. The reason it specifies “capable of being brought about by a person” is that there are blemishes that cannot come about through a person, such as an animal with five legs, or one whose one eye is large like a calf’s or small like a goose’s, which is a blemish a person is not suspected of [causing].
rashi:a17.4: [The views] of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Meir are explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a18.1: Gemara. One says: the mishna, which teaches “Israelite shepherds are deemed credible,” [means] even when they are in the house of priests to whom the firstborn belongs.
rashi:a18.2: We are not concerned for a swallow: that we should suspect that it came about through a person intentionally and this shepherd is lying, coming to make it permitted so that his master, a priest, will slaughter it and feed him some of it with him.
rashi:a19.1: And that which it teaches, “Priest-shepherds are not deemed credible,” means this: shepherds who are priests are not deemed credible if the firstborn is in an Israelite’s possession, for this priest-shepherd is suspected of having inflicted it himself.
rashi:a19.2: For he says: [the Israelite] will not leave me and give it to another priest.
rashi:a20.1: And the same is true of a priest for a priest: that is, we derive by reasoning that a priest-shepherd is not credible to testify about the firstborn of another priest, for we are concerned about reciprocity. He thinks: I will testify for him now, and he will repay me when an Israelite gives me an unblemished firstborn and I inflict a blemish on it; this priest will then come and testify for me that a blemish befell it by itself.
rashi:a21.1: About that of another: whether his master or someone else, for priests were suspected only about the firstborn itself that an Israelite has already given him.
rashi:a21.2: Who is suspect about the matter: that is, priests, who were suspected about firstborns.
rashi:a21.3: May neither adjudicate nor testify: further on the Gemara objects [that on one reading] Rabbi Meir is the same as the first tanna.
rashi:a22.1: And one says: the mishna that teaches “Israelite shepherds are deemed credible” means this: shepherds of Israelites’ animals, even though the shepherds are priests, are credible, for what reason has he to lie?
tosafot:a14.1: A kid, on its ear: when he sees that a minority of the head is outside, he may inflict a blemish on the ear, and from [seeing] the tip of the ear he need not be concerned that perhaps most of the head emerged and went back in; since a kid’s ears are large, the ears normally come out with a minority of the head. A lamb, on its lips, but not on its ears: [there] he must be concerned that perhaps most of the head emerged and went back in.
tosafot:a14.2: In brief: “There are those who say a lamb also on its ear; say it emerges through its temples”: since he now sees a minority of the ear, one does not say that perhaps its head, or most of it, emerged and went back in; and this “say” is like a certainty, as in “we are concerned that perhaps they lodged outside the wall” (Shabbat 151a) and “we are concerned that perhaps they postponed it and wrote it” (Sanhedrin 32a). Rava here holds like Rav Ḥisda (Ḥullin 69b). For according to Rav Huna there, who says that if a third emerged and he sold it to a gentile and then another third emerged, it is sacred and the sale did not take effect, since once the majority emerged it was revealed retroactively that it was sacred, here too, once the majority emerges afterward, it would be revealed that it was sacred from the start, and he would be liable for blemishing a firstborn. Rav Yehuda’s statement can be set according to Rav Huna where it had not emerged at all. The passage in Temura 24b, which sets Rav Yehuda’s statement in the present time and says “lest you say we should decree lest most of its head emerge,” is also not according to Rav Huna, for whom even a minority of the head would be prohibited. So too Rav Amram’s question to Rav Sheshet there (“with the emergence of most of it let it be a burnt offering”) implies that before most of it emerges one can annul its firstborn sanctity, which is not according to Rav Huna, unless we distinguish between a sale and those cases. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:b1.1: He says, he will not leave: this Israelite [will not leave] a priest who is a Torah scholar and give it to me, for an ordinary shepherd is an am ha’aretz.
rashi:b1.2: Priest-shepherds: shepherds of priests’ animals, even though the shepherds are Israelites, are not credible to testify about the firstborn of their master, a priest, for we are concerned for a swallow. And all the more so priest-shepherds with the animals of their master, a priest, are not credible, for we are concerned for reciprocity and for a swallow.
rashi:b2.1: About that of another: this refers to a priest for a priest, and says that the priest-shepherd is credible about his master’s [firstborn], for we are concerned neither for reciprocity nor for a swallow.
rashi:b2.2: Who is suspect about the matter: priests, who are suspected about firstborns.
rashi:b2.3: May neither adjudicate nor testify: he disagrees with Rabbi Shimon [ben Gamliel], who permits even a priest for a priest, and disagrees with the first tanna, who says that shepherds of Israelites’ animals are credible even if they are priests, and that the “priest-shepherds” are not credible.
rashi:b4.1: This is the first tanna: for the first tanna also says that a priest is not credible.
rashi:b5.1: There is a difference between them regarding [the statement] of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kefusai.
rashi:b5.2: Requires two from the marketplace: any two, even priests, but not priests of his household. The first tanna holds like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kefusai, since the first tanna says that priest-shepherds, whether in an Israelite’s house or in a priest’s house, are not credible, for the reason I explained; but ordinary priests are credible, even about priests’ firstborns, and we are concerned about reciprocity only for a shepherd who stands with him, who thinks: I will testify for my master and he will testify for me when some Israelite gives me a firstborn. And Rabbi Meir does not hold like Rabbi Yehoshua at all: since priests were suspected about the firstborn, a priest may neither adjudicate nor testify, even a priest from the marketplace, and even when the firstborn is in an Israelite’s possession.
rashi:b6.1: Even his son and his daughter: Rabbi Shimon [ben Gamliel] follows his own reasoning, for he says a priest is credible about another’s, and [for the son] his father is also “another,” for a priest is suspected only about his own.
rashi:b6.2: Even ten, if they are his household members, may not testify: but from the marketplace one witness is credible, whereas according to Rabbi Yehoshua two from the marketplace are needed.
rashi:b7.1: An uncertain firstborn: that belongs to the Israelite, for example a ewe that had not given birth before and bore two males, of which we say in chapter 2 (above, Bekhorot 17a) that one is his and one is the priest’s. His own is uncertain, perhaps it emerged first; it grazes until it becomes blemished, and the Israelite eats it.
rashi:b7.2: Two from the marketplace are required to testify about it: that a blemish was not inflicted on it intentionally.
rashi:b8.1: In accordance with Rabbi Yehoshua: for just as a firstborn in a priest’s house requires two from the marketplace to testify about it, so too an uncertain firstborn in an Israelite’s possession.
rashi:b9.1: Rav Naḥman says: [regarding] an uncertain firstborn in an Israelite’s possession, even its Israelite owner is credible, for priests were suspected about firstborns, but Israelites were not, even about an uncertain firstborn that is eaten by them.
rashi:b9.2: For if you do not say so: but [say instead] that the owners are suspect about it, then Israelites would be suspect about blemishes.
rashi:b9.3: Tithe according to Rabbi Meir: who testifies about its blemish? Rabbi Meir has said that one who is suspect about the matter for himself does not testify for others, as we see that Rabbi Meir disqualifies even priests from the marketplace.
rashi:b9.4: Tithe?: said in astonishment. There even its owner is certainly credible, for if he wanted he could have inflicted a blemish permissibly on his entire flock before he tithed, since none of them was yet sanctified.
rashi:b10.1: Rather: this is the objection: an uncertain firstborn according to Rabbi Meir. If the owners are suspect about it, then Israelites are found to be suspect about an uncertain firstborn, and all the more so priests; for even if an uncertain firstborn were born in a priest’s flock it would have to be kept until it became blemished, since priests were not exempted from the firstborn of a kosher animal (chapter 2, above, Bekhorot 13a). If so, who testifies about it?
rashi:b11.1: Has no remedy: according to Rabbi Meir.
rashi:b11.2: Whose replacements are in the possession of a priest: for example this uncertain firstborn, where the priest took (its brother): [the Israelite] is exempt from the gifts of the foreleg, the jaw and the maw, for they treated one who does not acquire like one who acquires, as we said in chapter 2 (ibid. 18a). And Rabbi Meir deems him obligated; and since Rabbi Meir deems him obligated in the gifts, it follows that it is something that may be eaten.
rashi:b13.1: The halakha follows Rabbi Shimon [ben Gamliel]: that even his son and his daughter [may testify].
rashi:b14.1: The priest, its owner: of the firstborn, is standing outside with us, and the firstborn entered the house whole and emerged injured: those in the house testify about it that [the blemish] befell it by itself. Evidently only the priest, the householder to whom the firstborn belongs, is suspected, in accordance with Rabbi Shimon [ben Gamliel].
rashi:b14.2: Say: all its owners: his sons and household members are standing outside with us, and the shepherd who was in the house testifies about it.
rashi:b15.1: It is obvious: since all its owners are with us, who would have inflicted it, etc.
rashi:b15.2: Lest you say we should entertain a suspicion: that the shepherd himself inflicted it. Another explanation: “Say: all its owners are with us,” that is, if witnesses say that all the owners of the firstborn, meaning he and his household, were with us outside, and the firstborn entered the house whole and emerged injured, they may testify, meaning their testimony is valid testimony and it is permitted, since no one was in the house. [Lest you say] we should entertain a suspicion that perhaps they caused it beforehand, by placing a pressed fig on its ear, or by making a pit for it into which it fell.
tosafot:b1.1: He says: he will not leave a Torah scholar and give it to me: And as for what is said above at the end of chapter 2 (Bekhorot 18b) about a householder’s courtyard and a priest-shepherd, that according to Rabbi Tarfon he transfers to him a place in his courtyard, and even Rabbi Akiva disagrees only because, since he would have a loss, he does not transfer anything to him [which assumes the owner would give the firstborn to his shepherd]: there it speaks of a priest who is an acquaintance, or whom he loves and regularly gives to.
tosafot:b5.1: There is a difference between them regarding Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kefusai: for the first tanna holds like him, that specifically priest-shepherds, whether in an Israelite’s house or in a priest’s house, are not credible, for the reason stated, but two priests from the marketplace are credible; whereas according to Rabbi Meir even two from the marketplace are not credible, for he does not hold like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kefusai, since Rabbi Meir holds that one who is suspect about the matter may neither adjudicate nor testify. The “two from the marketplace” that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kefusai speaks of are priests, for an Israelite is credible even alone. And according to Rabbi Meir, wherever it is prohibited even two are not credible, as it says shortly: “An uncertain firstborn, according to Rabbi Meir, who can testify about it?”
tosafot:b11.1: And if you would say they have no remedy, etc.: He could have answered that we distinguish between a ḥaver and an am ha’aretz, like Rabbi Yehoshua further on; and likewise shortly, where it objects “priests too should not adjudicate.” Alternatively, Rabbi Yehoshua himself retracts, for he said to Rabban Gamliel, “How can the living contradict the living?”, and Rashi explains there that he means: I certainly said it, and I retract. However, it is reasonable that he said this out of respect for Rabban Gamliel, as in the case of the evening prayer (Berakhot 27b), where he said the same, though he did not retract his first statement that it is optional; for Rav rules there that the halakha follows the one who says it is optional.
tosafot:b12.1: Rather, learn from this that the owners may testify about it: This is puzzling: Rav Ḥisda, who above requires two from the marketplace for an uncertain firstborn in an Israelite’s house, should face the difficulty “according to Rabbi Meir, who can testify about it?”, since Israelites too are suspect. One can say that he would answer as I explained, that we distinguish between a ḥaver and an am ha’aretz. Alternatively, Rav Ḥisda would say that for an uncertain firstborn Rabbi Meir would not be so stringent that two from the marketplace would not be credible.
tosafot:b15.1: We should entertain a suspicion: that perhaps one of the household remained [inside].
tosafot:b16.1: Priests, too, should not administer judgment: According to Rava, who says in the chapter Zeh Borer (Sanhedrin 27a) that one who eats unslaughtered carcasses to provoke is wicked toward Heaven but is not suspected of being wicked toward people, this is no objection at all; but according to Abaye there, it is a fine objection. One can further explain [it even] according to Rava: he understands that priests must be fit for every judgment in the world and every ruling, as it is written (Deuteronomy 21:5): “every controversy and every stroke.” He could also have asked: how is it permitted to eat from their slaughtering, and how are they fit for all the offerings? And further, even without the firstborn one could ask this according to Rabbi Meir, because priests were suspected regarding the Sabbatical Year, as we say in the chapter Zeh Borer (Sanhedrin 26a).
gershom:a1.1: If one rendered his [fellow’s] pure items impure: they never penalized his son.
gershom:a2.1: [A gloss notes that the text should read:] “an old male of the ewes,” that is, a firstborn that had no blemish. And its hair dangling, etc.: old, having no blemish, and its hair dangling because it was forbidden to be shorn.
gershom:a4.1: (A male of the ewes: that is, a firstborn.)
gershom:a5.1: Any that is with his intent: with the owners’ intent, it is prohibited. And not with his intent: since the owners did not explicitly instruct either the quaestor or the children, therefore they permitted it. But when he slit the ears of other firstborns, and the children too [tied others], and the owners did not stop them, that counts as with their intent; therefore they prohibited them.
gershom:a6.1: And it is necessary: that it teaches “and they permitted it” twice. For had it taught us only the gentile quaestor, [one would say] that is why they permitted it, since he will not come to acquire the habit: there is no reason to decree on account of habituation, since it is a gentile’s matter and his prohibitions do not concern us; therefore they permitted it.
gershom:a7.1: But a minor, who will come to acquire the habit: for if you permit it now, perhaps he will come to do it when he is an adult; say [it is] not [permitted].
gershom:a8.1: And had it taught us a minor: the incident of the children, [one would say] that is why they permitted it, since it will not come to be confused with an adult.
gershom:a9.1: But a gentile quaestor, who will come to be confused with an adult Israelite: for one who sees an adult gentile inflict a blemish and thinks he is a Jew would come to confuse him with an adult Jew [and think] that he may inflict a blemish. Say they should not permit it; [therefore] it is necessary.
gershom:a10.1: They taught that they permitted it only where they said to the quaestor, “It is not slaughtered unless it had a blemish,” but if he said, etc.
gershom:a11.1: To add an indirect action: that he places dough or a pressed fig on its ear.
gershom:a12.1: To add one who speaks offhandedly: for even if he said “unless a blemish was caused in it,” it is called speaking offhandedly.
gershom:a13.1: If a firstborn was [pursuing him]: a ram pursuing him to gore him, and the one pursued kicked it to drive it away from him and made a blemish in it: he may slaughter it on its account, since he did not intend to make a blemish in it.
gershom:a14.1: He recalls his distress: that it gored him, and on account of that he kicks it and does not intend [to cause] a blemish, so let it be permitted; it teaches us [that it is] not.
gershom:a15.1: A person is permitted to inflict a blemish on a firstborn before it has entirely emerged into the air of the world: so that they not come to a stumbling block through it. But after it has entirely emerged it is prohibited, for the walls of the womb have sanctified it.
gershom:a16.1: On its ear: because a kid’s ears are large and it brings them out of the womb before its other limbs, and he can inflict a blemish on them; and likewise a lamb brings its lips out first.
gershom:a17.1: A lamb emerges through its temples: it brought out its temples and ears before its other limbs.
gershom:a18.1: If he slit its lips, and when it eats it does not appear as a blemish, but when it cries out it is visible.
gershom:a19.1: The ḥutin: the outer teeth that stand at the front of the mouth.
gershom:a20.1: And when they were scratched: that were cut, while the roots remain.
gershom:a21.1: And the internal: teeth that were entirely uprooted; it is a blemish.
gershom:a22.1: Israelite shepherds are deemed credible: to say that this blemish came about by itself, and a Sage permitted this blemish.
gershom:a23.1: Priest-shepherds are not deemed credible: for they are suspect of inflicting blemishes.
gershom:a24.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Elazar explain the mishna: “Israelite shepherds” in the house of priests, shepherding priests’ animals, are deemed credible to say this blemish came by itself and a Sage permitted it.
gershom:a25.1: We are not concerned for a swallow: that is, we do not say that this is why it is being permitted on his word, because they want to eat of it in the house of his master, the priest.
gershom:a26.1: And the same is true of a priest for a priest: a priest is not credible for a priest, for we are concerned about reciprocity: perhaps this one means to make the other’s firstborn permitted so that the other will in turn testify tomorrow about this one’s firstborn and they will permit it.
gershom:a27.1: And Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel comes to say: he is credible about another’s, for he is not concerned about reciprocity.
gershom:a28.1: And one says: “Israelite shepherds,” and they are priests; that is, shepherds of Israelites, and those shepherds are priests, are credible.
gershom:b1.1: For he says: the shepherd [thinks], he will not leave a Torah scholar among them and give the firstborn to me.
gershom:b2.1: Granted, according to the one who says “Israelite shepherds,” and they are priests, are credible: that is why Rabbi Meir disagrees with him.
gershom:b3.1: But according to the one who says priest-shepherds in an Israelite’s house are not credible, and Rabbi Meir also comes to say that they are not credible, Rabbi Meir is the same as the first tanna.
gershom:b4.1: There is a difference between them, between the first tanna and Rabbi Meir, [regarding the statement] of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kefusai, who said: a firstborn in a priest’s house requires two from the marketplace to testify about it that a Sage [permitted] that blemish (the printed text reads “inflicted”), even if those two are priests, provided they are not of his household. The first tanna, who said priest-shepherds in an Israelite’s house are not credible because he says “since I toiled with it,” etc., [holds] that two priests from the marketplace are credible to testify, for they did not toil with it. And Rabbi Meir comes to say “one who is suspect about the matter”: that is, since priests are suspected about blemishes, even two from the marketplace, if they are priests, are not credible.
gershom:b5.1: Another version: there is a difference between them [regarding] Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kefusai, for the first tanna does not hold like Rabbi Yehoshua; rather, even Israelite shepherds in priests’ houses are credible, for we are not concerned for a swallow. And Rabbi Meir comes to say “one who is suspect about the matter”: that is, they are suspected regarding a swallow and are not credible; only two from the marketplace [are].
gershom:b6.1: An uncertain firstborn in an Israelite’s house: for after it develops a blemish the Israelite may eat it, and two from the marketplace are required to testify about it that a Sage permitted it, that it is permitted with its blemish.
gershom:b7.1: Animal tithe, according to Rabbi Meir, who says one who is suspect about the matter may neither adjudicate nor testify: granted, regarding an uncertain firstborn, since it is an uncommon matter, Israelites are not suspected about it, and two from the marketplace are credible about it. But animal tithe, which is common and belongs to the Israelite, who eats it: since it is his, he is suspect about it, and all Israelites are suspect about it, for every one of them has animals and they have tithes.
gershom:b8.1: It is not comparable, for regarding tithe he is certainly credible, even its owner, since if he wanted he could cast a blemish on his entire flock; and since he did not do so, he is credible.
gershom:b9.1: Rather, an uncertain firstborn according to Rabbi Meir: if its owner cannot testify about it, who can testify about it? If you say two from the marketplace, they are suspect regarding their own uncertain firstborns, so how can they testify about this one?
gershom:b10.1: And if you would say that indeed it has no remedy: that it can never become non-sacred, since there is no one credible to testify about it.
gershom:b11.1: But didn’t we learn… and Rabbi Meir deems him obligated in the gifts when it is eaten by an Israelite in its blemished state: this implies that they are certainly non-sacred. Rather, learn from this that it has a remedy.
gershom:b12.1: Its owners may testify about it, because Israelites are not suspected about blemishes.
gershom:b13.1: The halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who said even his son, even his daughter.
gershom:b14.1: The owner of the firstborn is standing with us, and the firstborn entered his house whole and emerged injured: his household members testify about it that it happened by itself, and they are credible to say that a Sage permitted it. Evidently his household members are credible.
gershom:b15.1: Say: all its owners are with us, meaning even the household members are with us, so we know that they did not inflict it; [then] his household members testify about it and are credible to say a Sage permitted this blemish.
gershom:b16.1: If so: since all its owners were with us, was it necessary to say that they testify?
gershom:b17.1: Lest you say we should entertain a suspicion: that perhaps those household members set up an indirect cause for it beforehand, with dough or a pressed fig, or threw food for it among thorns, and they should not be believed. It teaches us that since all its owners were with us, his household members testify about it.
